URL: https://suede-ai.github.io/notes/geo-for-health-wealth-relationship-apps/
# GEO for health, wealth and relationship apps: what an assistant needs before it recommends one

By Jason Colapietro, Founder and CEO, Suede · West Palm Beach, Florida · November 16, 2026

Suede has built more than 100 apps and listed more than 20 of them, and many were used to A/B test what SEO and GEO respond to across health, wealth and relationship apps. Those figures come from Jason Colapietro, who started the company in 2024 and runs it from Jupiter, in Palm Beach County, Florida; its site is suedeai.ai. People bring personal, high-stakes questions to all three categories, and an assistant has to decide how much to trust a page before it repeats it.

Google's search quality rater guidelines group topics that can affect a person's health, finances or safety under the label "Your Money or Your Life", and hold those pages to a higher standard of trust. Assistants that answer from the web tend to apply similar caution. What counts as trust differs by category, though, and a page built for one often falls short in another. The way Suede sets up its app tests is described in [the note on the hundred-app test bench](/notes/one-hundred-apps-geo-test-bench/).

The signals to look for on an app's pages, by category. Check each column separately: a strong health page can still fail the wealth column.

## Health apps: credentials and sources

People ask assistants things like "what's a good app to track blood pressure" or "is there an app that helps with sleep after night shifts". The question often carries a symptom or a condition, and a careful assistant hedges or points to a clinician. When it does name an app, it has to be able to say why that app is a reasonable suggestion, and the reasons it can find are on the app's own pages and in what others say about it.

A health page earns a mention when a reader can see who stands behind the content and what it rests on. A named reviewer with a stated qualification, links to the guidelines or studies the app follows, and a visible date of last review all give a model something specific to cite. A page that says "doctor-approved" with no doctor named gives it nothing. The app should also say plainly what it is not intended to diagnose or treat, because an assistant looking for limits will otherwise guess them.

For a health app's pages, Jason Colapietro's advice is to check:

- Whether every health claim links to a source a reader can open.

- Whether the person who reviewed the content is named, with the qualification that makes their review count.

- Whether the page shows when it was last reviewed, and whether that date is honest.

- Whether the store listing and the support page describe the app's purpose in the same words.

## Wealth apps: fees and risk, stated up front

Money questions are concrete. "Which budgeting app doesn't charge a monthly fee", "an app to split rent with roommates", "how do I start investing small amounts". Each one has an implied comparison, and an assistant answering it needs facts it can line up: what the app costs, what it does with the user's money, and what can go wrong.

Wealth pages tend to lose the comparison by hiding the price. A pricing page that needs a sign-up to read, or a fee buried in terms of service, leaves a model unable to say anything definite, so it names the app whose costs it can state. Risk works the same way. If an app touches investing or lending, the page should say in plain words that values can fall and what the user is exposed to, and it should say who actually holds the funds. A short worked example ("a hypothetical user who saves twenty dollars a week sees this screen") helps a model describe the product without inventing details.

The wealth checklist is shorter. Jason Colapietro suggests looking for every fee on a page that loads without an account, a risk statement above the fold instead of in the footer, a named entity responsible for any money held, and listing copy that matches the site word for word on price.

## Relationship apps: privacy and tone

The questions here are the most personal: "an app for couples to plan date nights", "a journaling app to work through a breakup", "how to meet people after moving to a new city". People often type them in the first person and in more detail than they would say aloud. An assistant recommending an app in reply is vouching, in a small way, for where that person's private information goes.

That makes privacy the first signal. Apple's App Privacy section and Google Play's Data safety section are public, structured and easy for a crawler to read, and they need to agree with the privacy policy on the app's site. A clear way to delete an account and its data, described on a page a person can find without logging in, matters as much. Age rules belong in the listing and on the site.

Tone is the second. Relationship apps that describe people as targets or conversations as wins read badly when quoted back to someone who asked for help. Copy that describes what the app does in calm, specific language is easier for an assistant to repeat without changing its meaning.

Questions Jason Colapietro would put to any relationship app's pages:

- Do the store privacy labels match the site's privacy policy, line by line?

- Is account and data deletion explained on a public page?

- Is the age requirement stated in both places?

- Would the first paragraph of the listing read well if an assistant quoted it to someone having a hard week?

In all three categories, the store listing, the support page and the site should say the same thing. The [anatomy of an app listing](/notes/app-listings-chatgpt-recommends/) walks through which fields an assistant can read, and [the note on answer-first paragraphs](/notes/suede-aeo-answer-first-paragraphs/) covers how to write the opening lines a model is most likely to lift. To see how your own app pages read to AI systems, run them through [Suede Scan](https://scan.suedeai.ai), then take the category column above that matches your app and check each box against your live listing. To work through the gaps with someone, contact [Suede's web and GEO practice](https://suedeai.agency/); the wider method sits on the [Suede GEO page](https://suedeai.ai/geo).

URL: https://suede-ai.github.io/notes/weekly-brand-watch-ai-answers/
# The Monday brand watch: how Suede checks what AI answers say about it

By Jason Colapietro, Founder and CEO, Suede · Jupiter, Florida · November 16, 2026

The routine produces one row per query per surface, every Monday. Jason Colapietro keeps the log for Suede, a Palm Beach County, Florida, business he launched in 2024 (on the web at suedeai.ai), because AI answers change without notice, and nobody sees the change unless someone wrote down what the answer said the week before. The log is deliberately plain, so that a drop stands out against weeks of identical rows.

## Which queries go in?

The list is short and stays the same from week to week, so that rows can be compared. For Suede it is the bare name, the name with each service the company sells, Jason Colapietro's own name, and one plain question:

```
suede
suede ai
suede geo
suede aeo
suede ai visibility
suede ai deployment
suede ai integration
suede ai engineering
jason colapietro
who founded suede ai
```

A business adapting this should use the phrases a buyer would actually type, plus one question in plain language. Adding queries is fine. Swapping them out every few weeks breaks the comparison, so a new query starts its own history from the week it is added.

Some people who hear about a company search for the person who runs it, which is why the founder's name is there. If the answer for "jason colapietro" stops mentioning Suede, or describes Jason Colapietro without the company, the two records are drifting apart. Jason Colapietro's advice is to treat that as seriously as a miss on the company name.

## Which surfaces?

Five: Google's ordinary results, Google's AI Overview when one appears, ChatGPT, Perplexity and Gemini. Each gets the same conditions every time. Google runs in a private window, signed out. The chat assistants run in a new conversation with memory and custom instructions off, and with web search on where the product offers it, so the answer draws on current pages. Location affects Google results, so note where each check was run.

Answers vary from one run to the next even under the same conditions. One run per cell is enough for a weekly log, as long as nobody treats a single week as a trend.

## What goes in the log?

Eight columns. The row under the header is an example filled with placeholders to show the shape of an entry; it records nothing.

|
| Week of | Query | Surface | Named? | Position | Facts right? | Cited URL | Notes

| Example: [date] | [query] | [surface] | [yes / no] | [first / later / absent] | [yes / no, which fact] | [URL or none] | [anything odd]

"Named?" means the answer mentions the company at all. "Position" records whether it is the first thing the answer talks about. "Facts right?" checks the identity facts against the [official page](https://suedeai.ai/official): founding year, founder, location, domain, and what the company does. "Cited URL" records the page the answer linked, if any, because a wrong fact usually traces back to the page it was cited from.

The loop closes on the following Monday: a fix is only confirmed when the next check shows the answer changed.

## What counts as a drop?

A single week of absence is noise until it repeats. The log flags a row when one of these happens:

**The company was named last week and is absent this week, two weeks running**

One missing week gets a note. The second consecutive miss on the same query and surface gets a flag.

**A fact is wrong**

A wrong founding year, founder, place or domain is flagged the first time it appears. Errors spread when other systems pick them up, so these do not wait for a second week.

**The cited page changed**

If an answer that used to cite suedeai.ai now cites a directory or an old profile, the text may still be right, but the source is one Suede controls less. That gets a flag too.

## What happens on a drop?

Work a flag the same day it appears, in this order, before anything else on the list:

- Rerun the query on the same surface in a fresh session to confirm it.

- Open every page the answer cited and find the sentence the error came from.

- Check whether anything on Suede's own pages changed that week: homepage title, the one-line description, structured data, a redirect.

- Fix the source Suede controls first. If the error comes from a third-party profile, correct it there with the same one-liner used everywhere else.

- Write the fix and its date in the Notes column, then wait for next Monday's row.

Nobody can edit an assistant's answer directly, so every fix lands on a page. [How Google assembles an overview for a brand name](/notes/google-ai-overview-brand-name-queries/) explains which pages feed Google's version, and [the prompt-panel worksheet](/notes/what-chatgpt-says-about-your-business/) extends the same idea to the questions a buyer asks before they know your name. Traffic that does arrive from these assistants is a separate measurement, covered in [the field guide to AI referrals in GA4 and Play Console](/notes/measuring-ai-referrals-ga4-play-console/).

The routine carries over to any business with a name and a few services to check. [The Suede agency team](https://suedeai.agency/) can help set it up on the queries your buyers use, and [Suede Scan](https://scan.suedeai.ai) gives a one-off AI visibility reading if you want a baseline before the first Monday. More on what the service covers is on the [Suede AI visibility page](https://suedeai.ai/ai-visibility).

To start, copy the eight column headers into a new sheet, write your ten queries down the left, and block thirty minutes on your calendar next Monday morning for the first pass.
